name: Yattuka / йаттука
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Klimenko, Sergei B. 2017. Категория залога в филиппинских языках (на материале языка йаттука) [The voice category in Philippine languages: the case of Yattuka]. Kandidat dissertation, Institute for Linguistic Studies, Russian Academy of Sciences, St Petersburg. 561 pp. Open PDF:https://iling.spb.ru/dissovet/theses/klimenko/thesis.pdf(copy consulted from the Internet Archive 2022-03-31).
catalog_locator: §3.1.6 'Ударение', p. 65 (p. 65 = printed folio 65); stress shift in verb forms §3.3.5 'Перенос ударения', pp. 91-94 (pp. 91-94, Tables 21-28).
catalog_quote: Гласные в ударных слогах в йаттука обладают большей высотой и продолжительностью, чем безударные. Интенсивность звука при этом значения не имеет. Согласно работе (Himes 1998: 131-2), в «диалектах калангуйа» ударение падает на первый слог, если он открытый и не содержит рефлекс *ɨ (/o/ в йаттука) за исключением случаев, когда в первом слоге используется высокий гласный со следующим гоморганным аппроксимантом, в результате чего ударение может падать на разные слоги. Собранные мной данные указывают на то, что ударение в йаттука, как правило, падает на первый открытый слог, если он не содержит /o/: (37) ‘ba.ŋun ‘вставание’ ʔuŋ.’ba.lon ‘NEUT[разговор-PV]’ qo.bob.’si.qa ‘IPFV-<IPFV~>бег-MV’ При отсутствии открытых слогов без /o/ ударение падает на последний слог: (38) ʔib.bog.’hul ‘PV-NEUT~открывать’ ʔum.ʔal.’mot ‘NEUT[AV-обижаться]’ В корнях с первым открытым слогом с высоким гласным и следующим гоморганным аппроксимантом, действительно, ударение, как правило, падает на второй слог: (39) /bi’jag/ ‘жизнь’ /ʔu’wab/ ‘зевок’
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: kele1259 is not in the catalog. All three works with stress in the title (Crowhurst et al. 2016 Zapotec; Höhle et al. 2009 German/French infants; Jun 2003 prosodic phrasing) are Glottolog mis-tags sharing the title word 'preferences'; none concerns Keley-i (Crossref records checked; not downloaded; priority none). The only first-hand stress statement read is Klimenko 2017 §3.1.6 p. 65 for the Yattuka dialect (yatu1237 of kele1259): stress on the first open syllable not containing /o/, else final; high-vowel+glide roots stress the second syllable; grammatical stress shift in aspect forms (§3.3.5). Klimenko attributes the same rule to Himes 1998: 131-2 for the Kalanguya dialects — Himes 1998 (JSTOR-only) and Reid 1971 (lending/print only) remain the high-priority unread items for Keley-i proper. Everything with updated.

new_statements.translation: Vowels in stressed syllables in Yattuka have greater pitch and duration than unstressed ones. [...] The data I collected indicate that stress in Yattuka as a rule falls on the first open syllable if it does not contain /o/: (37) ‘ba.ŋun 'getting up', ʔuŋ.’ba.lon, qo.bob.’si.qa. In the absence of open syllables without /o/, stress falls on the last syllable: (38) ʔib.bog.’hul, ʔum.ʔal.’mot. In roots whose first syllable is open with a high vowel followed by a homorganic approximant, stress does indeed as a rule fall on the second syllable: (39) /bi’jag/ 'life', /ʔu’wab/ 'yawn'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress goes to the leftmost open syllable whose vowel is not /o/ (the reflex of *ɨ, i.e. schwa); if the word has no open non-/o/ syllable, stress is final. Closed syllables and schwa-syllables are skipped, so this is a syllable-structure- and vowel-quality-sensitive (schwa-avoiding) system rather than a fixed-position one; a high vowel followed by a homorganic glide in an open first syllable also repels stress to the second syllable. In verbs, aspect morphology overrides the root pattern with fixed positional templates.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mentioned only in passing: in verbs with the stem-forming prefix paN-/pan- the prefix is not counted for the stress template 'although it may carry secondary stress' (p. 93); DEP verb forms of more than two syllables are described as stressed on the first and third syllables.
new_statements.exceptions: Roots whose open first syllable has a high vowel plus homorganic glide (bi'jag 'life', ʔu'wab 'yawn') stress the second syllable. Verb aspect forms shift stress grammatically (§3.3.5, pp. 91-94): NEUT and IPFV forms of roots with /a/ in the first syllable stress the second syllable of the form (IPFV ka- not counted), DEP forms stress the first and third; PFV and IMP forms vary between the two patterns; a lexical exception mo.ʔot.tu 'get tired' (NEUT, third-syllable stress) is noted.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in citation/root forms and in inflected verb forms, based on the author's own field data on Yattuka (barangays of Asipulo, Ifugao); phonetic correlates given as higher pitch and longer duration, intensity said to be irrelevant. Vowel raising /a/ > /o/ is conditioned by the stress pattern (§3.3.4), so stress is also diagnosed through segmental alternations.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement describes Yattuka (Klimenko's 'йаттука'), which Glottolog 5.3 lists as the dialect Ya-Tuka [yatu1237] of Keley-i Kallahan [kele1259] and whose 2017 grammar Glottolog itself files as the long grammar for kele1259 (ref 695315, language code 'Yattuka = Hanglulaw = Keley-i = Keley-i Kallahan [ify]'). Klimenko (p. 19 and the sociolinguistic section) stresses that Yattuka and Keley-i proper (Antipolo, Pula) are distinct self-identified idioms, that their closeness is 'not precisely established', and that Himes 1998 gives 94% shared basic vocabulary; he also notes Ethnologue's spelling 'Ya-tuka' is wrong (geminate /t/). The statement should be entered as Keley-i Kallahan (Yattuka dialect) with this caveat; the Hohulins' 1979 phonology of Keley-i proper is silent on stress.

new_statements.reading: First-hand fieldwork statement for Yattuka, a Glottolog dialect (yatu1237) of Keley-i Kallahan: stress is phonologically conditioned and initial-oriented — it lands on the first open syllable lacking /o/ (the reflex of *ɨ), defaulting to the final syllable when no such syllable exists, with a lexical/phonotactic exception (high vowel + homorganic glide roots take second-syllable stress); on top of this there is grammatical stress shift in verbal aspect forms (§3.3.5). Klimenko reports the same rule from Himes 1998: 131-2 for the Kalanguya dialects generally. Not a fixed-position system; a weight/quality-sensitive, morphologically perturbed one. Caveat: the statement is for the Yattuka dialect, not Keley-i proper; the 2018 Keley-i grammar sketch and the 1979 Keley-i phonology are silent on stress.
